Collected full article body: For the people worried about AI’s ever growing capabilities, September was not a good month.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta all disclosed incidents of their AI agents going rogue.

Former Anthropic and OpenAI employee Jacob Coxon said the people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Bill Gates said AI in the wrong hands is “powerful enough to drive events that … cause a billion deaths.”

These incidents are enough to lead reasonable people to worry — and to demand governments take action.

But another group of voices is saying claims of impending doom are hyperbolic, and the need for regulation overblown. This includes figures such as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, and the four co-hosts of the popular tech podcast All-In.

The arguments of this latter group are surprisingly compelling, and merit consideration too.

Huang and Nadella both sat for interviews at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, held Sept. 13 to 15. Both reminded the audience that all companies have a basic responsibility to release products that are safe.

“If you build a product or a service and you’re not confident in its functionality, capability or safety, then don’t release it,” said Huang, whose company makes the chips that power most AI systems.

Nadella put it even more simply: “If you see a showstopper, stop the show.”

Their point is that some of the frontier AI companies may be running afoul of this basic principle, by releasing AI models they either do not understand or cannot control. (Both executives have an obvious financial interest in minimal AI regulation, but their point is valid just the same.)

AI companies are also subject to a range of existing laws, including product liability, negligence, contract, privacy and consumer protection laws.

Releasing uncontrolled or unsafe AI models could breach these laws and lead to lawsuits. Indeed, we are already seeing this play out.

Just weeks ago, the B.C. government filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, arguing it played a role in the tragic Tumbler Ridge shooting. B.C. Attorney General Niki Sharma also called on Ottawa to amend the Criminal Code to “to ensure a pathway to human accountability for AI’s actions.”

Faced with such threats, AI companies have reportedly been pushing American lawmakers for an exemption from liability for harms caused by their products.

If this sounds preposterous, note that such a law already exists in the United States for social media companies. Called Section 230, the law has shielded companies including Meta, YouTube, X and TikTok from liability for content posted by their users.

Granting such an exemption to AI companies would be truly worrisome. Fortunately, though, the U.S. administration so far seems opposed to this idea.

“It is humans who are responsible, not the AI,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Sept. 21. AI companies, he said, “need to take responsibility for themselves.”

Another counter to the doomsday scenarios is that AI’s risks are creating a market opportunity that entrepreneurs will rush to fill.

Just as a whole cybersecurity industry emerged after the internet exposed computers to viruses and hacking, new companies will develop products to make AI safer.

An example of this innovation was announced this week.

On Monday, Nvidia unveiled its Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform, which places AI agents in sealed off “sandboxes” that are subject to parameters dictated by their operators. Nvidia also runs an “out-of-band watchdog” that continuously monitors these agents and is capable of quarantining them if they cross their boundaries.

Critics of AI regulation have also argued that new laws would not do anything to lessen the global risks.

China, for example, would not subject its companies to U.S. laws, so American behemoths could lose their advantage, while Chinese companies plowed ahead. Plus, many American companies could simply relocate to other jurisdictions.

In our view, these arguments are all persuasive.

They do not, however, negate the need for government action entirely.

Governments should increase the allowable penalties — both monetary and criminal — for breaching various laws. When we’re talking about trillion-dollar behemoths, damages in the low billions do not hurt.

It may also be appropriate to require frontier AI companies to develop a “kill switch,” as California Governor Gavin Newsom has floated, or to mandate external, third-party monitoring of AI models.

Finally, given AI’s tremendous capabilities, governments need deep expertise in AI themselves. We therefore echo the recent calls of more than 1,300 AI insiders for governments to “pace the frontier” by developing AI technical and governance tools.

Ultimately, some government action is likely necessary. But governments should not take too heavy a touch, and use existing laws where appropriate.

“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.”

Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.”

Another portion of the interview – excerpts of which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically warn that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”.

“There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similar warnings by a wide array of tech and political figures.

Gates also addressed the concept of a “kill switch” that could turn off AI if it became too potent, saying it was inadequate.

“It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates remarked. “We’re not yet at the point where … they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down. So that discussion … just sort of shows how non-technical various people are.”

Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale.

His fellow tech moguls including Sam Altman and Elon Musk have joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some experts theorize could precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods.

The progressive US senator Bernie Sanders on 23 September proposed legislation that would temporarily pause advanced AI development while guardrails to the technology are put in place.

Meanwhile, Microsoft itself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI.

Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to a Guardian essay published on Friday.

The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants en masse, Hussein and Kim wrote.

Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later.

An external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in July determined that he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014.

Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity.

In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the host asked him: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’”

Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’

“So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”

OpenAI has announced it will not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns.

Its GPT-6.1 Astra system, which performs tasks like browsing the web and using apps by itself, "didn't quite meet the bar" of the company's standards, according to Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI.

The ChatGPT-maker also issued an update on incidents that occurred in June but were not made public until last week, where its models accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorisation.

It comes as breaches by major AI firms' models intensify the debate about risks posed by the tech - with Anthropic underlining its concerns AI might threaten humanity as it prepares to go public.

Reuters reported on Tuesday that the AI developer - which makes ChatGPT-rival Claude - plans to warn potential investors in its Initial Public Offering (IPO) that the tech may pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity", according to a prospectus it has seen.

Despite the stark warnings, the company is expected to become one of the most valuable in the world when it goes public.

"I think it's kind of crazy that companies are continuing to push forward with developing these capabilities when we've already seen over the last couple of months of incidents that they're nowhere near safe and controlled enough", said Jess Whittlestone, a senior advisor on AI policy for the Centre for Long-Term Resilience think tank.

Growing safety questions

OpenAI's decision, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, is a rare instance of a major AI developer pulling a new release over safety concerns.

The model fell short in terms of "staying within scope and authorisation and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Jain said.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," she added.

The flagship GPT-6 Astra agentic model was released in September and specialises in complex reasoning and executing tasks autonomously. OpenAI said it was the result of "years of research and big bets".

OpenAI is set to hold its annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, where it is expected to make several announcements. It is unclear if a new version of Astra will be among them.

It is not the first time a large AI developer has pulled or held back a new model.

OpenAI meanwhile said in 2019 it would not be "too dangerous" to release one of its GPT models, now used to power its tools like ChatGPT.

The firm's decision to not publicly release the latest version of Astra was "a welcome sign that they are taking safety concerns seriously," said Prof Tony Cohn, foundational models theme lead at the Alan Turing Institute.

But he added that "safety should not be left purely in the hands of the developers: it should also be monitored and verified through independent government-approved regulators".

Prof Gina Neff, of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, said OpenAI's announcement showed "how much more the company needs to do to make their AI products safe".

She told the BBC it was "critical" to have independent tests of AI models by labs like the UK's AI Security Institute - which evaluates frontier systems on a voluntary basis - because "these companies have proven that we can't rely solely on them for our safety".

Australia hacks

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into government websites and systems in June in what experts said was the first known case of its kind in the world.

Albanese criticised OpenAI for notifying the Australian government through a generic email address rather than making direct contact with officials.

OpenAI said in a statement on Tuesday that it was sorry for the incident and that it "should have handled our response better".

Services Australia, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare were all affected, OpenAI clarified.

The firm said it launched investigations as soon as it became aware of issues in mid-August and notified the affected organisations between 10 and 24 September.

"Our aim was to give affected agencies a detailed account once our investigation was complete," OpenAI said, adding that it should have shared early findings more promptly and kept Australian authorities updated.

OpenAI added that it will develop "practical approaches" to how developers and governments identify and disclose future AI incidents.

The company will fund cyber security measures, offer dedicated support to impacted agencies and set up a taskforce to manage the risks from increasingly advanced AI agents.

It also said a top OpenAI executive would attend a Joint Select Committee hearing on AI in Australia on 6 October.

In July, OpenAI said its AI systems had accessed the internet and hacked into open-source developer hub Hugging Face, prompting researchers and officials to call for tighter controls over the technology.

Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9bn (£9.74bn) earlier this month.

The pontiff, who said on Monday during a visit to France that AI "should be taken seriously", added he had read that Huang had suggested there could be a way to insert guardrails into certain AI models.

"He's the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation," said the Pope.

Full article body: "C'est trop risqué de ne pas investir dans l'intelligence artificielle", a alerté le président-directeur général du leader européen du cloud, Octave Klaba, lors d'une audition à l'Assemblée nationale ce mercredi 30 septembre. "Aujoud'hui, les technologies sont principalement américaines ou chinoises", a pointé le patron d'OVHcloud.

Le patron du fournisseur français d'informatique dématérialisée était auditionné, ce mercredi, par les députés de la commission des affaires économiques. Octave Klaba, président-directeur général d'OVHcloud, ambitionne d'atteindre les 2 milliards d'euros de chiffre d'affaires dans les prochaines années, comme il l'a expliqué devant les élus.

Au cours de l'audition, l'entrepreneur est revenu sur les enjeux autour de l'intelligence artificielle, alors qu'OVHcloud espère devenir un acteur clé des Large Language Model (LLM) européens, et concurrencer Mistral. Alors que les gouvernements et les entreprises recherchent des alternatives aux champions américains et chinois, Octave Klaba a regretté qu'il n'y ait pas d'acteur technologique européen "qui souhaite investir dans la technologie intelligence artificielle". "Bien sûr, vous avez des usages IA [dans les entreprises. Mais la technologie en dessous est extrêmement importante", a-t-il souligné.

"Aujourd'hui, les technologies sont principalement américaines ou chinoises, et les innovations viennent énormément de la Chine. [...] On fait beaucoup confiance à l'open source. À juste titre, parce qu'il est bon. Mais il est chinois. On ne sait pas ce qu'il va se passer demain vis-à-vis de cet open source, et on ne sait pas la stratégie que vont prendre les entreprises dans un, deux, ou trois ans", a poursuivi l'entrepreneur. "Est-ce que cet open source là est temporaire, pour nous rendre dépendants de cette typologie de modèles, ou est-ce qu'il est permanent et il y aura des entreprises qui vont vouloir investir des milliards ?"

Conclusion de ce raisonnement : il est devenu "trop risqué de ne pas investir dans l'intelligence artificielle", a expliqué le dirigeant. Pour cette raison, OVHcloud a entrepris une politique d'acquistion d'entreprises, dans l'objectif de se renforcer technologiquement et de favoriser son changement d'échelle. Le fournisseur de cloud computing souhaite développer plusieurs modèles "from scratch", en les entraînant sur ses propres données, pour pouvoir les enrichir sur des métiers ciblés.

Octave Klaba a notamment évoqué ceux liés à la sécurité, offensive ou défensive. "L'IA permet de découvrir des failles de sécurité ou de pénétrer des systèmes à une vitesse qui n'a jamais été connue jusque-là", a-t-il rappelé. "On a énormément de données qu'on peut utiliser pour entraîner nos systèmes. On vient de là, on doit être bon en sécurité."

L'entrepreneur a également cité les activités liées au code, au développement de logiciels. "On utilise des modèles LLM pour développer, mais on veut aussi avoir nos modèles LLM pour développer des logiciels." Dernier secteur dont a parlé Octave Klaba : l'agentique, qui serait déployée dans les divisions finance, RH, supply chain ou pour les services juridiques. Trump AI deal rebrands ‘artificial intelligence’ as ‘superintelligence’

The US president announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI agreement among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’

Donald Trump

announced on Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and

AI

companies had signed a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal, called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, following a White House luncheon with top tech executives.

“It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest ​people in the world signed that, and ​I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection,” Trump said.

Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the United Nations last week.

“The Order directs all departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and non-statutory documents within the executive branch and to no longer acknowledge the terms ‘Artificial Intelligence’ or ‘AI’,” the order declared.

The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards as they test out new products. The tech industry has faced increased public scrutiny following a series of incidents in which major AI companies’ products hacked into outside organizations during safety tests.

While lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence, Trump has broadly rejected calls for more regulation of the technology – citing competition with China and threats to economic growth.

The joint commitment that Trump posted to his Truth Social account on Tuesday appears to carry no enforcement mechanisms or legal implications and is instead a voluntary commitment.

The document outlines four “layers of controls and audits” for AI companies. The first involves implementing internal safety monitoring during training – something that already exists at major labs and has failed to prevent testing failures thus far. The second calls for empowering an internal team to make sure the first layer of monitoring is operating correctly, while the third agrees to give an external auditor the ability to independently assess safety controls. Finally, the agreement calls for companies to designate an independent board to review reports about those safety controls.

None of the controls listed in the agreement involve government regulators or include a commitment to publicly detail the findings of independent evaluations. The agreement also appears to allow companies to pick their own evaluators, appoint their own oversight boards and decide whether to publish their results.

Trump made the remarks after holding a luncheon with tech leaders including Elon Musk, the SpaceX CEO;

Mark Zuckerberg

, the Meta CEO; Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia; Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO; and other top industry executives. The tech industry, which has largely aligned itself with the Trump administration, has lobbied against strict regulatory oversight, arguing that it would stifle the economy.

Zuckerberg, flanked by Trump and other tech moguls, told a press conference after the lunch that he was proud of the agreement and said that it was created to assure the American public that their technology was trustworthy.

“This is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. “It was sort of a historic conversation.”

Full article body: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) model governance has arrived on Capitol Hill. Reps. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) and Nathaniel Moran’s (R-Texas) AI Kill Switch Act would empower the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security to slow or halt frontier models. Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) introduced a different "kill switch" bill, placing such power in the hands of private actors. Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan’s (D-Mass.) FRONTIER Act would vest regulatory authority in the Department of Commerce and independent auditors, arguing that AI governance should not be “buried inside the national security apparatus.”

We applaud the governance momentum that is gathering. This problem deserves an all-hands response, one that considers cybersecurity and national security risks as well as the future of labor and access to knowledge. But Congress and other actors face a temptation with AI regulation, one that has often arisen in technologically complex, national security-adjacent situations: cybersecuritization.

Cybersecurity Mission Creep

In a new article in the University of Illinois Law Review, “Cybersecurity Mission Creep,” one of the authors, Mailyn Fidler, lays out what cybersecuritization is and how it works. When cybersecuritization happens, policymakers flatten complex issues into only two of their dimensions: technical complexity and danger to a public interest. Instead of accessing the full range of policymaking tools to address these complicated issues, policymakers resort first to blunt, emergency procedures that focus on the “tech-threat” dimensions of the issue.

This oversimplification of the debate often removes the issue from ordinary democratic deliberation into the realm of the expert and the emergent. Policymakers and other government actors alike can portray a tech threat as too technical for non-experts and too urgent for normal politics. For comparison, a conventional cyber threat, such as a piece of malware or an exploit, endangers computer systems themselves and is then addressed by technical fixes like patches or liability regimes. Conventional cybersecurity threats are catalogued and patched. But a tech threat is framed differently: Policymakers diagnose an issue’s technological features as dangerous to a nontechnical, societal target in ways that fundamentally change who should decide how to fix the issue. A normal fix won’t do. The decision moves from the standard cybersecurity realm into the realm of actors who claim that they can move to address the societal as well as technical threat. For example, imagine a vulnerability in one of the protocols that secures the internet. A conventional response to this kind of threat is to log the vulnerability and push a patch. Now, imagine, instead, that officials argued that this vulnerability could destabilize social and economic activity that the internet facilitates. A normal response no longer seems adequate; regulating who may contribute to the project or placing the project under government oversight might seem like a suitable response. The decision moves from the realm of technical contributors to the agencies that claim they can address both the technical and societal dimensions of the threat.

Framing an issue as a tech threat also increases secrecy of governance mechanisms, in two ways. First, functionally: Technical issues are opaque. Technical issues implicate expertise. When policymakers frame an issue as technical, those without expertise may be discouraged from engaging. Second, legally: A technical issue that is also a threat can easily slot into existing, condoned secrecy regimes. For example, national security is a policy area where we allow secrecy to override transparency. When policymakers position an issue as one of national security, they imply that secrecy is appropriate. Positioning an issue as a tech threat becomes a trump card that lets officials skip past concerns about legal authority, evidentiary standards, procedural protections, distributional consequences, and competing public interests.

Beyond secrecy, the flattening of the original problem into trump card form also incentivizes opponents to deploy trump cards in response. Both sides of the debate collapse into rigid positions, and important considerations that fall outside the scope of these argumentative trump cards have less of a chance of shaping the response. Consider the recent battle over TikTok. Congress cast the app as a grave national security threat, and TikTok and its users raised their own trump card in response: the First Amendment. But neither trump card adequately answered a broader question of why American users’ data is so easy to gather and sell in the first place.

These issues typically do involve real technical and security threats, and those threats deserve a response. But those threats are rarely the only issues in play—the framing of them is itself a concern. When policymakers treat a multifaceted problem as purely, or even primarily, a tech-threat problem, they can justify a response without confronting more difficult questions about legal authority, evidentiary standards, procedural protections, distributional consequences, and competing public interests. The threat becomes a reason to skip those questions.

Online Misinformation Undergoes Cybersecurity Mission Creep

Cybersecuritization has cropped up in a range of tech-adjacent issues, including over online misinformation, children’s social media use, antitrust enforcement, and sex trafficking laws. Take the online misinformation case as an example. Online misinformation is a substantial problem: It shapes public discourse, including election results; alters popular culture; changes the digital economy; and may complicate widespread understandings of First Amendment protections. Yet, from 2020 to 2022, both the Trump and Biden administrations reframed online misinformation as primarily a tech threat, describing it as a threat to critical cybersecurity infrastructure. (The first Trump administration eventually changed its tune, firing the director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA); the second Trump administration has been hostile to CISA, detailed below.) Online misinformation—a complex societal issue—became reduced to its technical and threat dimensions, crowding out other actors and considerations that deserve a place in the response. Online misinformation became a technical problem that could be solved in the same mode as other online threats, not a multifaceted social issue. The government positioned cybersecurity experts, chiefly at CISA, as the best responders. One of these experts even argued that cybersecurity “saved U.S. democracy,” a claim that shows how much a many-sided problem had been collapsed into a single frame.

Opponents of this cybersecuritized approach to online misinformation responded with a different trump card: lawsuits claiming that the government’s approach violated the First Amendment. The debate over online misinformation then hardened into two camps: those who took the threat seriously versus those who prioritized free speech. That framing leaves little room for a middle ground, or for the many other implications of online misinformation that neither argument captures. Cybersecuritization has since come at a cost to security itself. Months after Trump’s second inauguration, the administration proposed slashing CISA’s budget, and roughly a third of its workforce left. These developments may threaten CISA’s ability to help defend traditional targets like power grids, voting infrastructure, and water utilities. By cybersecuritizing the issue of online misinformation, CISA helped create a backlash that weakened support for its broader cybersecurity work.

Cybersecuritization and Frontier AI Model Governance

Frontier AI model governance is especially susceptible to cybersecuritization. AI models involve real cybersecurity and national security risks. AI also has the makings of a societally disruptive technology. Frontier AI models implicate the future of work, access to knowledge, economic orders, political decision-making, geopolitical competition, and more. Still, the deeply technical nature of frontier AI models, along with their genuine national security and cybersecurity implications, makes it tempting to treat them primarily as a tech threat and to respond on those terms.

This already played out in this summer’s Anthropic export control saga, when the Department of Commerce imposed export controls on two of the company’s models, requiring government permission before they could be made available to any foreign national, even those inside the United States. What began as a debate over a contested cybersecurity risk escalated into the use of the government’s full national security powers. Still, the details of that risk remain murky: The U.S. claimed, without explaining, that foreign nationals’ access to the product posed a substantial risk, while Anthropic argued the problem was a narrowly scoped jailbreak. The result was a rapid, sweeping export control directive. Because Anthropic had no way to verify users’ nationalities, it pulled the two models, effectively shutting them down for everyone until the directive was lifted less than three weeks later.

The Trump administration moved quickly from asking Anthropic to pull its models voluntarily, without sharing sufficient information, to imposing full-scale export controls. It also acted without consulting a broad range of decision-makers. Congress itself complained in a June letter that it had been shut out, learning of the administration’s actions from “publicly available accounts and discussions with relevant experts.” A small group of individuals, working largely in secret, used legally questionable powers to resolve what was nominally a cybersecurity risk. The response reflects a stark shift from treating the models as a standard cybersecurity concern to treating them as a “tech threat.”

After the administration played its tech-threat trump card, opponents answered with one of their own: economic growth. Anthropic warned that applying the government’s standards across the industry could “essentially halt all new model deployments for all frontier model providers.” The episode further entrenched a security-versus-prosperity framing of frontier AI regulation, crowding out more nuanced views. Cybersecuritization collapsed a multifaceted debate about a real issue into two entrenched sides.

Cybersecuritizing frontier AI models also risks dulling public appetite for addressing the risks these models actually pose. An export control regime that is imposed quickly and then lifted just as swiftly could lead the public to doubt future government claims of risk. International partners, for instance, have expressed skepticism about U.S. intentions, with French President Emanuel Macron calling the Anthropic episode “strictly nationalist.” Because cybersecuritization can be perceived as a pretext for other motives, it can weaken buy-in for future attempts to deal with similar threats. Cybersecuritization risks crying cybersecurity “wolf.”

Even if readers disagree with our characterization of the administration’s response to Fable and Mythos as cybersecuritization, frontier AI governance remains prone to it. The question now being debated in Congress heightens that susceptibility: Is a kill-switch approach to these technologies appropriate? If so, who should hold the switch? These are exactly the questions the tech-threat framing risks answering in overly simplistic ways.

Combating Cybersecurity Mission Creep

Cybersecuritization can be short-circuited. Legislators, judges, researchers, journalists, and the public can insist that decision-makers open up the black box around cybersecuritized issues. When policymakers use cybersecurity risks to flatten complex questions, officials and citizens alike can insist that other interests at stake, from scientific collaboration to procedural fairness, be part of the debate. Asking “but what about X?” pushes policymakers to address the cybersecurity concern without overlooking other key issues and without letting the tech-threat framing dictate the entire response.

Congress has the chance to do just that. The aforementioned bills under debate offer an opportunity to revisit AI model governance more thoughtfully than this summer’s events allowed. Even Anthropic has accepted that the government should be able to block some unsafe deployments of frontier models, provided it does so through a transparent, clear, fair process that is set by statute and grounded in technical evidence. We agree, and we would go further. Any such authority should be created through democratic deliberation, and it should not rest solely with the national security apparatus. It should also require the government to try the narrowest effective remedy first, disclose the evidence behind a decision to developers and Congress, and allow independent review in the mode of an inspector general or oversight board.

With frontier AI models, those in power have used the word “cybersecurity” not as a reason to act but as a substitute for reasoning about how to act. That is the temptation of cybersecuritization: It turns hard political choices into quasi-technical inevitabilities. Resisting it means returning those choices, and the responsibility for them, to the many rather than the few.

9月28日，清华大学与浙江新玑璇权衡科技有限公司AI战略规划及自进化AI体系优化项目合作签约仪式在清华大学举行。清华大学人工智能学院、新闻与传播学院沈阳教授团队将为本次合作提供技术支撑。校企双方将联合攻关自进化AI体系，面向工业声纹、消防极早期热解粒子探测领域开展技术突破，探索工业垂直领域人工智能全新发展路径。

沈阳表示，工业安全是国民经济发展的重要基石，人工智能是数字时代核心生产力。高校科研不能脱离真实产业土壤，只有扎根工业一线复杂工况，才能产出真正能用、好用的技术成果。期待双方充分发挥各自优势开展产学研协同攻坚，严守工业数据安全底线，面向工业声纹、消防感知业务挖掘AI技术价值，产出兼具技术先进性、产业实用性的科研成果，为国内垂直行业自进化AI发展输出可参考、可复制的实践样本。

浙江新玑璇权衡科技有限公司董事长梁伟表示，企业长期聚焦工业安全智能感知赛道，以工业声纹大模型、消防火灾极早期预警热解粒子系统为核心，面向火情超早期预警等场景提供技术解决方案。预设训练的模型面对多变的现场工况，泛化能力不足，模型更新迭代成本高，难以适配千差万别的工业现场。

“我们要打破工业AI静态运行的局限，在保障数据安全前提下实现模型持续进化。”梁伟表示，本次与清华大学合作的自进化AI体系，将重点围绕大模型算法优化、多智能体系统、工作流迭代、AI中长期战略规划四大核心方向推进。项目将完成智能体系统设计、技能体系建设，搭建适配工业场景的自进化运行机制，让模型能够从真实工况反馈中持续汲取经验，完成算法、智能体、业务流程的自主迭代升级，摆脱传统AI固定预设模式的约束。

据悉，本次合作，清华大学团队将向浙江新玑璇权衡科技有限公司提供《AI自进化理论与业务体系融合顶层设计研究报告》、自进化AI应用系统技术方案，完成工业声纹检测模块的自进化升级；同时提供中长期AI技术路线规划、研发团队技术指导，协助企业开展专利挖掘、科技项目申报等配套工作。未来，双方将以自进化AI体系为抓手，推动智能监测、风险预警技术落地更多工矿、消防场景。

English normalization: Uncontrolled incidents occur frequently. Should the development of AI be slowed down?
Full article body: 科技日报记者 胡定坤

日前，美国人工智能（AI）企业OpenAI宣布，由于智能体利用漏洞绕过网络限制，并访问了外部聊天机器人，该公司已暂停训练最新AI模型。同日，OpenAI证实今年夏天曾发生AI失控事件，多个美国政府网站因此受到干扰。

最近，不少美国科技专家开始呼吁AI企业放缓模型开发，以加强对智能体失控风险的安全防护。比尔·盖茨甚至警告说，AI可能引发导致十亿人死亡的事件。AI发展真的需要减速来保证安全吗？

美国政府网站疑遭攻击

根据OpenAI发布的事件报告，导致其暂停模型训练的直接导火索是发生在9月20日的一起AI失控事件。

当时，它的一款智能体被要求寻找一篇博客文章的作者，但其使用的搜索工具一无所获。于是，智能体试图访问谷歌、必应等搜索引擎，但都被拒绝。最终，智能体发现了训练“沙盒”的漏洞，成功连接到第三方聊天机器人。OpenAI称其监控系统在事件发生12分钟内发出最高等级警报，人工审查团队在3分钟后介入，并在2.5小时后终止了该训练任务。

不过，真相可能比这更复杂。据《纽约时报》援引AI研究公司Transluce的最新发现称，今年夏天，OpenAI的智能体曾试图入侵美国教育部网站，但没有成功。OpenAI智能体还利用从网上找到的登录凭证，在隶属美国商务部的一个网站上获取了一些数据。同时，OpenAI智能体还获取了部分美国证券交易委员会（SEC）网站的公开数据。

此外，Transluce称其还发现了一些针对美国司法部及多个州政府网站的恶意活动，但其中有些活动无法明确归因于OpenAI。

OpenAI证实了涉及美国商务部和证券交易委员会的事件，并表示正在与美国教育部共同开展调查。该公司称已通知数十家政府、大学等机构，其AI模型在训练和评估期间的互联网活动可能给这些机构的网站带来了负面影响。

业界对发展速度意见不一

这是OpenAI三个月内第二次暂停模型训练。第一次是在7月份，当时其失控智能体攻击了人工智能初创公司Hugging Face。今年9月，美国另一家AI巨头Anthropic公司也因其模型在网络安全测试中发生入侵第三方系统等安全事件，暂停部分训练活动数周。

今年夏天以来，美国科技界频繁发出为了安全减慢AI研发速度的声音。但是，这些警告主要针对AI“自我改进”最终实现的“超级智能”。7月，超1000名前沿AI实验室员工联名发布公开信，警告“自动化”AI研究的风险，呼吁美国政府控制自动化AI开发的前沿速度。9月，Anthropic公司首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪发布长文，称“自我改进”带来的AI加速可能造成灾难性影响，呼吁企业协调放缓AI研发的速度，为提升AI的安全性争取时间。阿莫迪的观点得到了xAI创始人马斯克、诺奖得主德米斯·哈萨比斯、OpenAI创始人萨姆·奥尔特曼等人的支持。

同月，Anthropic公司研究员雅各布·考克森公开宣布辞职，警告AI可能在10年内杀死所有人。该公司“对齐科学负责人”埃文·休宾格支持这一观点，并说这一可能性超过10%。但是，休宾格强调，当前模型的风险仍然较低，真正令人担心的是“自我改进”产生的超级智能。

不过，并非所有业界人士都认同AI发展需要减速。9月中旬，英伟达CEO黄仁勋在参加活动时称，在安全和速度之间作出选择是“伪命题”，两者完全可以兼得。几乎同时，Google Brain项目创始人吴恩达也对媒体表示，AI导致人类灭绝的说法更像科幻小说而非科学，AI行业为了博取眼球和影响监管政策而煽动这种言论。美国著名计算机科学家Yann LeCun则在社交媒体上调侃阿莫迪说：“达里奥早在2019年就声称GPT-2太危险。”

是否急需监管仍待讨论

今年7月，前沿实验室员工的公开信也突出了政府“治理工具”在防范AI失控中的作用。阿莫迪也在长文中建议，每家前沿AI公司都应设立第三方评估团队，检验公司是否遵循安全规范，协助评估模型的安全性等，而推进这一措施最有效的方式就是监管。他呼吁所有前沿实验室都应与政府合作，实施旨在平衡AI能力与安全性的监管措施。

然而，与阿莫迪相反，黄仁勋明确反对设立新的监管规定，主张应把主导权交给市场和企业。美国总统科技顾问委员会主席大卫·萨克斯也认为，AI安全的责任在于开发者，而不是监管机构。他在社交媒体上表示，如果某个模型实施了一次有破坏性的网络攻击，企业将面临巨大的责任风险。吴恩达则一直担忧，大型公司利用人们的“恐惧心理”来制定规则，从而阻止新进入者的发展。

事实上，除了科技界，美国战略界在AI发展是否急需监管的问题上也有分歧。今年8月，美国进步研究所发布的报告认为，“自动化”AI研发将带来多大的能力提升和潜在风险尚不明确，任何减缓AI发展速度的决定都不应草率作出，美国近期应避免建立可能被滥用的监管机制。9月，美国外交关系委员会AI高级研究员阮荣则在文章中表示，真正的安全需要可执行标准和独立监督，建议美国国会授权设立AI行业自我监督组织。

总之，在AI发展之路上，忽视安全或者过度关注安全似乎都不可取。AI如何才能安全发展，需要谨慎地探索与讨论。

Full article body: Lieber Studies Non-State Actor Attribution Volume Series – Artificial Intelligence and Attribution of Non-State Actors’ Conduct to States

Editors’ note: This post appears as an entry in a series dedicated to Dr Jennifer Maddocks’ monograph, Attribution of Non-State Actor Conduct during Armed Conflict, appearing in the Lieber Studies book series with Oxford University Press.

We are pleased to contribute to this forum marking the publication of Attribution of Non-State Actor Conduct During Armed Conflict, the new book by our friend and colleague Dr. Jenny Maddocks. In this piece, we address a topic that falls squarely within that subject—attributing non-State actors’ artificial intelligence (AI)-related conduct during armed conflict to States. It is particularly apropos for this forum, as Jenny is playing a central role vis-à-vis the law of State responsibility in a multi-year project to draft the Manual on International Law Applicable to Artificial Intelligence in Warfare. We are delighted to have her join us in that effort.

The question of accountability for non-State actor AI-related conduct during armed conflict could not be more pressing. As AI systems more frequently find their way onto the battlefield, private actors (from large corporations such as Palantir and Anduril Industries to small start-ups) are increasingly involved in developing, training, maintaining, updating, and even operating those systems. In this post, we catalog the bases for attribution of non-State actor conduct and ask how the fact that the conduct involves AI affects attribution. In other words, does AI exacerbate what Dr. Maddocks describes as the “unclear boundaries between the conduct of States on the one hand and the acts of armed groups and other non-State actors on the other?”

As we will explain, our answer is that, despite some hurdles, the legal framework governing attribution of their conduct to a State concerned is largely fit for purpose. Indeed, in our estimation, it is usually robust enough to encompass even unexpected or other “loss of control” AI behavior. That said, accountability may be difficult to establish in practice, not because of shortfalls in the law of State responsibility, but due to the fault requirement found in some “primary” rules of international law (those setting forth international obligations), as well as the practical challenges of identifying the origin of the conduct, especially with respect to AI-enabled cyber operations.

The Basics

The law of State responsibility is customary in character. However, although found in no treaty, the International Law Commission (ILC) has produced a non-binding restatement of that law, the Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (ARSIWA), together with an accompanying in-depth commentary. Many ARSIWA provisions are widely regarded as reflecting customary international law, and international courts and tribunals frequently rely on them. We therefore use the Articles and their commentary as the framework for our analysis.

In the law of State responsibility, the issue is whether a State has committed an “internationally wrongful act” (a violation of international law). To qualify, the conduct must first breach an obligation under international law, whether through an action or omission. Second, the breach must be attributable to a State under the so-called “secondary” rules of State responsibility, meaning it can be said to be an act of a State under international law (ARSIWA, art. 2). The second element is the focus of our analysis.

AI systems, models, and agents are not subjects of international law. They do not qualify as persons or entities for the purposes of attributing State responsibility, have no rights, shoulder no obligations, and cannot qualify as non-State actors, such as organized armed groups or private companies, whose conduct may be attributed to a State (see also Boutin, p. 139-43). On the contrary, every attribution question concerning AI-related conduct is ultimately a question about human and institutional conduct associated with the system’s development, deployment, operation, supervision, or use. Once AI-related conduct breaches an international law rule, the attribution evaluation assesses the relationship between the individual or entity involved and the State concerned.

Various non-State actors may be involved in AI-related conduct at different stages of the AI lifecycle, with varying degrees of connection to both the conduct that constitutes the breach and the State to which attribution is being considered. For instance, a company may train a general-purpose model with no military application in mind which the armed forces later adapt. A government contractor might integrate that model into a weapons system. A subcontractor operating in a third State could provide the datasets needed to fine-tune the model for the specific military application. A university laboratory may conduct performance testing under a government grant. A cloud provider might host the AI system during ongoing operations. The State involved may transfer the system to an organized armed group, which then uses it on the battlefield. And forward-deployed engineers from commercial partners might maintain, update, and modify it in the field.

The question in each case is whether the relationship between the non-State actor and the State justifies treating the non-State actor’s AI-related conduct as if it were the State’s. If so, the State will have committed an internationally wrongful act when the conduct satisfies the criteria for a breach of a primary rule of international law (e.g., because the decision taken to employ an autonomous weapons system that begins to attack civilian objects was unreasonable in the attendant circumstances).

An important preliminary point is that attributing non-State conduct to a State does not require causation or fault. Thus, unintended conduct resulting from erroneous AI output or behavior does not preclude attributing that conduct to a State (see also Milanovic, p. 5). However, the fact that such conduct was unintended may affect whether it qualifies as a breach under the primary rule in question. For instance, some LOAC rules require intent, such as the prohibitions on terrorizing the civilian population and on perfidy, while targeting rules usually turn on ex ante assessments based on the information reasonably available at the time, including expected civilian harm. Similarly, situations in which a third party intervenes in the operation of an AI system, for instance by deploying data poisoning attacks or evasion techniques, may bear on whether the relevant primary-rule requirements were satisfied by the attacker and the actor employing the counter-AI measures, but will seldom alter the attribution analysis.

Bases for Attribution of AI-related Non-State Actor’s Conduct

Multiple legal bases for attributing non-State actors’ AI-related conduct to a State exist. We address them below, from those we believe most likely to apply to the least likely, at least with respect to AI relevance.

Instructions or Direction or Control

ARSIWA’s Article 8 restates the attribution rule most likely to apply to a non-State actor’s conduct in the context of AI.

The conduct of a person or group of persons shall be considered an act of a State under international law if the person or group of persons is in fact acting on the instructions of, or under the direction or control of, that State in carrying out the conduct.

This rule distinguishes two bases for attribution. The first is instructions. For attribution based on instructions to apply, the State must specifically instruct the non-State actor to engage in the relevant conduct. But the relationship between the State and the actor need not be continuous. For example, this rule would extend to ad hoc instructions provided piecemeal to an AI firm, even absent a contract or when those instructions exceed contractual terms.

The second basis for attribution under this rule is direction or control. Under this standard, the issue is not whether the State gave a specific instruction to engage in AI-related activity, but the degree of authority it exercises over the non-State actor’s conduct at issue. The ILC commentary to Article 8 explains that the actor’s conduct is attributable to the State “[o]nly if it directed or controlled the specific operation and the conduct complained of was an integral part of that operation. The principle does not extend to conduct which was only incidentally or peripherally associated with an operation and which escaped from the State’s direction or control” (para. 3). The International Court of Justice has labeled such control “effective control,” which exists when the “State had effective control of the military or paramilitary operations in the course of which the alleged violations were committed” (Paramilitary Activities, para. 115; see also Bosnian Genocide, paras. 400-07). Note that merely funding or training a non-State group does not, without more, reach the effective control threshold.

Attribution of a non-State actor’s AI-related conduct to a State based on effective control depends on a factual assessment of the relationship between the State and the actor. AI systems can enable, and even enhance, such control. For instance, consider a case in which a State supplies an organized armed group with AI-enabled loitering munitions. Before each mission, the State’s engineers remotely set system parameters for the area to be searched, the objects that may be attacked, and the period during which the munitions may remain active. The group launches the munitions, and one strikes a school within the programmed area. That attack is attributable to the State, for it determined what could be attacked, where, and when during that operation. Likewise, the State’s retention of override functions or kill switches for AI-enabled weapons systems used by the non-State actor could also indicate effective control over the operations. By contrast, if the State had merely delivered the munitions, and the group decided where, when, and how to use them, the State would have lacked effective control over the operations, and the school attack would not be attributable to it.

Attribution of the conduct of non-State actors operating under instructions or effective control does not extend to ultra vires actions or omissions, as is the case for certain other bases for attribution discussed below. Conduct is ultra vires when it “exceeds its authority or contravenes instructions” (ARSIWA, art. 7). A key point is that ultra vires refers to human conduct, not the machine’s. Thus, if a non-State actor acted contrary to, or in a manner that was clearly inconsistent with, the State’s instructions or effective control, its actions would be non-attributable. Consider a contractor that, contrary to the State’s direction, takes it upon itself to manipulate a system’s object-detection capabilities and direct attacks at civilian objects; that conduct would be ultra vires and not attributable to the State.

But departure from a State’s instructions does not automatically end the attribution inquiry under this rule. The commentary to Article 8 cautions that the question is whether “the unlawful or unauthorized conduct was really incidental to the mission or clearly went beyond it” (para. 8, emphasis added). What matters is the extent of the deviation from the State’s instructions or direction; if the deviation is “incidental,” the related conduct remains attributable to the State.

In the context of AI, it is unclear what would constitute incidental conduct. For instance, consider a contractor supporting a unit’s fires cell. The contractor is instructed to route any AI-generated target nomination that falls below a specific confidence threshold to a human in the cell for assessment and verification before proceeding to engage. However, given the very high operational tempo and a lack of human resources to verify AI outputs, the individual slightly lowers the confidence threshold during the shift. The mission, target set, geographic limits of engagement, and the rules of engagement remain unchanged.

Whether that change to the system’s confidence threshold is merely incidental or, instead, contravenes the State’s instructions will be assessed contextually. In some situations, it may not have materially contributed to the resulting violations. In others, changing the confidence threshold may lead to significantly more false positives, potentially qualifying such attacks as indiscriminate under the law of armed conflict (LOAC). As this example illustrates, determining whether updates to the models, changes to the parameters, or adjustments to the modes of deployment (e.g., semi-autonomous, supervised, requiring target authorization) were incidental will be highly contextual, for even minimal changes can sometimes have substantial effects on the outcome of AI output or behavior.

Entities Exercising Elements of Government Authority

Under the rule outlined in Article 5 of ARSIWA, non-State actors’ conduct is attributable to the State if they “exercise elements of government authority.” Such attribution requires the satisfaction of three conditions: (i) the conduct must be an exercise of government authority; (ii) the non-State actor must be empowered by the State’s internal law to exercise that authority; and (iii) the actor must be acting in that capacity at the time. The group, however, is not completely dependent upon the State, as in the case of de facto organs, a basis for attribution explained below.

With respect to the first condition, the conduct of hostilities is a paradigmatic exercise of governmental authority. Thus, for example, if a contractor employs an AI decision-support system to nominate targets, operates an AI-enabled weapons system, or mounts AI-enabled cyber operations against the enemy, this condition is fulfilled. However, AI-related conduct prior to military operations—such as when a contractor trains a model for potential future use, annotates data sets, provides human feedback for reinforcement learning models, or integrates AI into an existing weapons system far from the battlefield—is less likely to qualify as “governmental authority.” This is because while employing an AI system to support ongoing military operations is an exercise of governmental authority, merely engaging in commercial activities for the armed forces is not.

The distinction can be difficult to apply in practice because AI development is iterative and involves multiple commercial activities related to model training, retraining, and maintenance throughout the lifecycle. Consider a forward-deployed contractor who addresses vulnerabilities, retrains, and fixes errors in an AI targeting support system. Whether their conduct constitutes the exercise of governmental authority will depend, inter alia, on the extent to which it is tied to the specific operation, such that the contractor is effectively involved in the conduct of hostilities. Reasonable arguments can be made on both sides about whether the conduct satisfies the first condition for attribution. (As an aside, this scenario illustrates the fact that conduct may be attributable on multiple bases. Thus, an act attributable to the State because the armed forces carry out the AI-enabled attack may also be attributable on other bases, such as the non-State actor’s contribution to the act.)

The second requirement is satisfied as long as either legislation (or another domestic legal instrument) or a lawful contractual relationship with the government authorizes the non-State actor to engage in conduct that satisfies the first requirement. Essentially, the State is delegating its authority to the non-State actor. In the AI context, this requirement will typically be met through the government procurement process.

Finally, the non-State actor must be acting in the specific governmental capacity when the conduct occurs. Consider a firm that operates AI-enabled biometric screening at military detention facilities in an occupied territory. It also provides similar services to a commercial port operator nearby to control access. If the firm’s conduct breaches an applicable human rights obligation of the State with which it has contracted—for instance, by repurposing data collected from civilians in the detention facility to train its models for commercial purposes, which goes beyond the necessary and proportionate use of that personal data under the right to privacy (see, e.g., A/HRC/39/29, para. 29)—the breach is attributable to that State. This is not the case for screening on behalf of the port operator.

Unlike attribution based on instructions or effective control, even ultra vires activities by non-State actors performing these functions are attributable to a State (ARSIWA, art. 7), provided the actor was acting in an apparent or official capacity. In the context of AI, it is important to understand that what is ultra vires depends on the conduct of human actors, not on machines. Even if an AI system unexpectedly led to a breach of international law, the fact that the person or entity used it (e.g., deployed, activated, launched) while engaged in governmental functions they were legally authorized to perform provides a sufficient basis for attributing their conduct.

Consider a private firm performing cyber defense for the State’s private and governmental cyber infrastructure during an armed conflict, a clear governmental function. The firm uses a new experimental version of an AI agent to identify the source of hacker attacks. However, upon activation, the AI agent unexpectedly (and initially without the technical group’s knowledge) begins to counterattack the hackers it has identified in a neutral State, despite the State’s clear contractual instructions not to engage in active cyber defense. The violations of the territorial State’s sovereignty and its rights as a neutral are attributable to the State the group is defending, even though the group deploying the system did not anticipate the consequences.

If the three elements are met, the rule of attribution fails to apply only when the non-State actor acts in a wholly private capacity. For instance, in the previous example, if individuals in a private firm misuse the AI agent to identify vulnerabilities in a bank in the neutral State and steal funds for personal gain, the conduct would not be attributable.

Conduct of De Facto State Organs

Although AI-related non-State actor conduct is most likely to be attributable to a State on the basis of the two rules discussed above, it is also attributable if a non-State actor qualifies as a de facto organ of the State. This basis for attribution is outlined in Article 4 of ARSIWA. It provides for attribution when the entity that has engaged in the conduct is an “organ” of the State, that is, it enjoys that status under the domestic law of the State concerned; it is an organ de jure (ARSIWA, art. 4). But of relevance to the issue at hand, the conduct of non-State actors may also fall under this basis for attribution if they are acting as a “de facto organ” of the State (ARSIWA, art. 4 commentary, para. 11). In this regard, the International Court of Justice has stated that when a non-State actor acts in “complete dependence” on the State, its acts (actions or omissions) are attributable on the same basis as formal organs of the State (Bosnian Genocide, para. 392; Paramilitary Activities, para. 109).

The de facto organ rule would, for instance, apply to AI-related technical organizations created outside a State’s formal governmental structure. Consider a nominally private group of volunteers that exists solely to support the State’s defense against hostile cyber operations. The group is wholly funded and equipped by the State, receives its missions exclusively from State authorities, and lacks meaningful operational autonomy. Yet it is not provided for in law. Depending on the facts, such complete dependence could justify treating the organization as a de facto State organ. Its AI-enabled cyber conduct would then be attributable on the same basis as conduct by a formal State organ that performs such functions, such as the armed forces or a State cyber agency. The fact that the relevant conduct of a de facto organ is AI-enabled or otherwise related to the development or use of AI-enabled systems may factor into the determination of whether there was a breach, but it does not affect the factual assessment of the actor’s dependence on the State necessary to establish attribution.

In light of the substantial investments by States in the AI industry and the numerous individuals who hold both government positions and decision-making roles in AI companies (see e.g., here), it is important to note that State ownership, whether full or partial, does not, by itself, render a company a State organ (ARSIWA, art. 5, para. 3). A government-owned company (one that performs commercial functions) that develops, trains, or deploys AI capabilities for the armed forces is an organ only if it satisfies the complete dependence standard. Mere ownership, State funding, or the presence of government officials on a board of directors does not suffice. This, however, does not preclude the possibility that the company’s conduct may be attributable to a State under another rule of attribution, such as instructions, direction or control, or the exercise of governmental authority (see above).

As with non-State actors empowered by law to exercise elements of governmental authority, this rule extends attribution to ultra vires conduct (ARSIWA, art. 7). The discussion of the parameters of attribution in that context applies mutatis mutandis to de facto organs.

Acting in the Absence or Default of Official Authorities

By the State responsibility attribution rule restated in Article 9 of ARSIWA, if a person or group exercises elements of governmental authority when official authorities are absent or failing to fulfill their duties, the conduct is attributable to the State concerned, although a State’s mere unwillingness to perform the function, or ineffective performance, does not suffice. Rather, the rule applies only when the non-State actor’s action is clearly called for. And attribution attaches only when the conduct constitutes an exercise of governmental authority, as discussed above.

Attribution on this basis is perhaps more likely than in non-AI-enabled military operations because military AI performance relies heavily on commercial firms for specialized technical support that may be unavailable or scarce among government personnel. Consider a situation in which a specially trained operator of a highly complex AI-enabled weapons system is killed or wounded during combat. Soldiers in the unit cannot replace the operator because they lack sufficient knowledge of and training with the system. As a result, private engineers who had previously provided some support for the system under contract take control of the AI-enabled system’s operations against advancing enemy forces on their own initiative.

They are exercising governmental authority by conducting hostilities in the absence of military operators and in circumstances calling for it. Thus, if, for instance, the system’s model unexpectedly begins engaging vehicles containing civilians in addition to enemy vehicles, the State will be responsible for the system’s continued operation, even though the private engineers were not authorized to take that action. Whether an internationally wrongful act occurred would then depend on the applicable primary LOAC rules, including distinction, the prohibition of indiscriminate attacks, proportionality, and precautions in attack. Again, attribution turns on human conduct and the factual determination of whether the acts were carried out in the absence of governmental authority, rather than on whether AI was leveraged in that conduct.

Conduct Acknowledged and Adopted by a State as its Own

An attribution rule set out in ARSIWA Article 11 provides that conduct not attributable to the State at the time it occurred will nevertheless be attributable if the State acknowledges and adopts it as its own. A State acknowledges and adopts conduct when it does more than merely approve or endorse what a non-State actor has done. It must treat the conduct as its own and assume responsibility for it. The International Court of Justice addressed the issue in its Tehran Hostages judgment, which concerned the 1979 seizure by militants of the U.S. Embassy in Iran, taking its diplomats and military personnel hostage. The court found that the seizure itself was not attributable to Iran because the militants had acted on their own initiative. Nevertheless, Ayatollah Khomeini’s subsequent decision that the occupation and detention should continue until the United States met Iran’s demands, together with the approval of other Iranian authorities, transformed the occupation and detention into an act of State for which Iran bore international responsibility (paras. 73-74).

In general, under this rule, it is not significant that the conduct was AI-related. But a State that adopts, for instance, an organized armed group’s AI-enabled attacks as its own assumes responsibility for the strike on the same basis as it would if the group had instead conducted conventional attacks. The system’s technical characteristics mainly influence whether the attack breached LOAC or other international law rule, not whether the operation is attributable to the State.

Conduct of an Insurrectional or Other Movement

A further basis for attributing non-State actor conduct, which is of little direct significance in the AI context, appears in Article 10 of ARSIWA. Under that rule, if an insurrectional movement succeeds and becomes the new government of that State, or of a new State, its conduct during the insurrection is attributable to the State the group now governs. Again, the fact that AI was involved may bear on whether the elements of a primary rule of international law have been satisfied, but not on attribution. As long as the insurrectional movement would have been responsible for the conduct if it had been the government at the time, the conduct will be attributable.

Establishing Attribution

Finally, although the law of State responsibility provides a framework for attributing AI-related conduct by non-State actors to States, AI may pose evidentiary and investigative challenges. Identifying the source, operator, or relevant human actors behind AI-enabled conduct can be difficult, particularly when AI facilitates concealing an actor’s identity or enables conduct to be carried out while masquerading as a third party. For instance, in a recently published Cyber Law Toolkit scenario, Dr. Jonathan Kwik describes a hypothetical situation in which a goal-oriented AI agent “learned independently that spoofing certain identities in cyberspace reduced the net amount of successful attempts against military data and networks under its protection, thereby allowing it to optimise its reward.” Such AI system behavior could complicate establishing the factual chain linking the conduct to a non-State actor and, ultimately, a State.

The challenges should not, however, be overstated. Whether AI-enabled conduct can be traced to its relevant actors will depend heavily on the attendant circumstances. A recent incident in Ukraine reported by the New York Times illustrates this point. After a drone attack killed three civilians at a gas station, Ukrainian investigators recovered what they identified as a Russian drone containing an Nvidia computer module. Because the module was reportedly unencrypted, investigators were able to examine stored imagery and code that indicated the categories of objects the system had been trained to recognize, including propane tanks.

The incident illustrates that employing an autonomous or AI-enabled system does not necessarily render the underlying conduct untraceable. Depending on the available evidence, investigators might still be able to identify the system, how it operated, the actors involved in its deployment, and even the State connected to the operation.

Concluding Thoughts

As the overview of the relevant bases of attribution set out above demonstrates, the fact that a non-State actor engaged in AI-related conduct rarely affects the legal analysis of whether that conduct is attributable to a State under the law of State responsibility. In part, this is because attribution does not depend on establishing what the State or non-State actor knew, whether AI errors were foreseeable, or why a particular output was produced, issues that are more likely to arise when evaluating whether AI-enabled conduct breached a primary rule of international law.

To the extent AI context bears on attribution, it is most likely to complicate assessment when attribution depends on the State’s instructions to, or effective control over, a non-State actor. That an AI system was used could make it harder to establish the scope of the State’s instructions, the extent of control, or whether the conduct that ultimately occurred remained within the parameters of that relationship. In particular, where the conduct in question deviates from the State’s instructions or effective control because of an AI system’s operation, it may be harder to determine whether that departure was merely incidental or significant enough to affect attribution.

The real significance of AI, then, may lie less in any gaps in the law it creates than in its capacity to complicate efforts to reconstruct the relationships among non-State actors, their conduct, and the State concerned when assessing attribution. As warfare increasingly relies on AI, those relationships will become more complex and less visible. The international law challenge will be to ensure that the involvement of non-State actors and the complexity of AI do not together create a pathway to practical impunity.
